newsitem.title: USA: Pilots' leaders deny backing down on regional jets.
newsitem.headline: Pilots' leaders deny backing down on regional jets.

text.p: American Airlines' pilots' union said on Tuesday it has no intention of softening its stance on the carrier's use of small regional jets, the thorniest issue in their bitter contract dispute.

Brian Mayhew, chairman of the Allied Pilots Association's negotiating committee, said the union gave up no ground on the issue at negotiations with management last week and would stick to its guns in the weeks ahead.
"We think we have a strong case on regional jets and we are staying with it," Mayhew said in a telephone interview.

Published newspaper reports have said the union's 18-member board last week dropped its insistence that all regional jets be flown by American pilots, opening the way for the airline's lower-cost commuter carrier American Eagle to use the jets.
Mayhew described the reports as "utter nonsense" and accused American's management of leaking false information in a bid to confuse pilots.

"At no time did APA negotiators ask for permission to move away from our proposal on the small (regional) jets. We did not ask for it nor did the board grant permission to change our position," he said. "It was not even discussed."
Pilots Association President Jim Sovich also said the reports were "patently untrue" and that the union's position had not changed.

American's 9,300 pilots, all of them Allied Pilots Associations members, walked off the job at midnight Friday but President Bill Clinton intervened minutes later, appointing a presidential board to help resolve the dispute. The move forced the pilots to return to work and pushes back any strike by 60 days.

The three-member presidential board will consult with the pilots' union and airline management and then offer a proposed solution within 30 days. If, after another 30 days, either side rejects the proposal and they are unable to strike a deal, the union would be free to take strike action, although Congress could pass a law imposing a settlement.
While the two sides have been unable to reach agreement on pay raises, the regional jets issue has proven even more difficult to resolove.

American wants to equip American Eagle with the 50-seat and 70-seat jets, but the pilots' union says it suspects management would use the planes to shift short-haul routes -- and pilots' jobs -- away from American Airlines and towards the commuter carrier, which uses pilots from another union.
Mayhew said he believes American plans to transfer between 2,000 and 3,000 pilots' jobs to American Eagle over a 10-year period if allowed to equip it with the regional jets.
He conceded that some union members are not convinced the issue is worth striking over but said the Allied Pilots Association would push the issue in upcoming meetings with the rank-and-file.
"Some of the pilots don't yet understand the full implications of regional jets and what the company plans to do with it," he said. "We'll fix that."
Officials at American Airlines declined to comment on the union's negotiating stance.
The company has insisted only American Eagle could operate the jets profitably.
